prediction.text: Coca-Cola says it uses derivatives, not speculation, to manage these risks, according to its 10-K. For currency, it uses forward contracts, options, collars, and swaps to hedge forecasted transactions like foreign-currency sales and purchases of inventory. These are generally designated as cash flow hedges. It also hedges the value of some net investments in foreign subsidiaries, using derivatives and foreign-currency-denominated debt, and it uses fair value hedges and swaps to manage interest rate and debt-related currency exposure. For commodities, the company says it uses derivatives to hedge some of its exposure to the prices of sweeteners, metals (aluminum), juices, PET plastic, and energy. Beyond derivatives, it relies on natural hedges from operating in many currencies and on pricing actions. It also manages counterparty risk by dealing with highly rated institutions and using netting agreements. The company cautions that these hedges are not complete, so large currency or input-cost swings can still hurt results. For specific notional amounts, hedge durations, or current positions, check the market risk and derivatives notes in the latest 10-K, as I'm not certain of the current figures.
